chapter_summary:
Database replication is a cornerstone of modern data management, critical for ensuring high availability, improving read performance, and providing robust disaster recovery capabilities. In PostgreSQL, replication involves maintaining multiple copies of your database, where changes made on a primary server are continuously propagated to one or more standby servers. This setup offers significant advantages. Firstly, high availability means that if your primary database server experiences a failure (hardware, software, or network), a standby server can quickly take over, minimizing service disruption. Secondly, replication allows you to distribute read workloads across multiple servers, scaling your application's ability to handle more queries without impacting the primary's write performance. Finally, replicated standbys serve as excellent candidates for disaster recovery, providing a geographically separate copy of your data that can be promoted in case of a catastrophic event affecting your primary data center.

PostgreSQL offers two primary categories of replication: physical and logical. Physical replication, often referred to as streaming replication, operates at the file system or block level. It works by streaming the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) records from the primary server to the standby servers. WAL records contain every change made to the database, ensuring that the standby can precisely reconstruct the primary's state. This method is highly efficient and guarantees an exact, byte-for-byte copy of the primary database. Physical replication is ideal for disaster recovery, read scaling, and providing a hot standby for failover. The main limitation is that the standby database is read-only and cannot be selectively replicated; it's an all-or-nothing copy of the primary.

In contrast, logical replication operates at a higher level, replicating data changes based on their logical representation (e.g., INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE statements) rather than physical WAL records. This method offers much greater flexibility. You can choose to replicate specific tables, schemas, or even entire databases, allowing for selective data distribution. Logical replication is particularly useful for major version upgrades, migrating data between different PostgreSQL versions, or integrating with heterogeneous systems. It also enables multi-master setups, though this is more complex. The trade-off is that logical replication can be more resource-intensive and might not be as performant as physical replication for very high-volume write workloads, and it doesn't replicate DDL changes automatically.

A crucial distinction in replication is between synchronous and asynchronous modes. Asynchronous replication, the default for PostgreSQL streaming replication, means that the primary server commits a transaction and proceeds with its work *before* receiving confirmation that the changes have been written to the standby server's WAL. This offers excellent performance on the primary but introduces a small window of data loss if the primary fails before the changes are propagated and flushed on the standby. For many applications, this small risk is acceptable due to the performance benefits. Synchronous replication, on the other hand, ensures that a transaction on the primary is not considered committed until it has been successfully written to the WAL *and* confirmed by at least one standby server. This guarantees zero data loss in the event of a primary failure, but it comes at the cost of increased transaction latency on the primary, as it must wait for network round-trips to the standby. Choosing between synchronous and asynchronous depends heavily on your application's specific RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and performance requirements.

The Write-Ahead Log (WAL) is the heart of PostgreSQL's data durability and replication mechanisms. Every change made to the database – every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL operation – is first recorded in the WAL before being applied to the actual data files. This ensures atomicity and durability, even in the event of a crash. For replication, the primary server continuously streams these WAL records to its standby servers. The standbys then replay these WAL records to keep their data synchronized with the primary. This continuous streaming and replaying process is what makes PostgreSQL's native streaming replication so robust and efficient. Understanding WAL is fundamental to configuring and troubleshooting any PostgreSQL replication setup.

screens.title: Introduction to Replication Concepts
screens.subtitle: Why replication matters, how PostgreSQL copies data, and the role of WAL

narration.text: In this lesson we establish a working mental model for replication in PostgreSQL. Replication means keeping multiple copies of your database so that writes on a primary server are propagated to one or more standbys. You will learn why teams deploy replication: to keep services available when hardware or software fail, to spread read traffic across servers so primary writes stay fast, and to maintain geographically separate copies for disaster recovery. We will also introduce two replication approaches — physical streaming and logical replication — and explain a crucial internal component, the Write-Ahead Log, which drives native streaming replication. To ground the idea, imagine a master chef who writes every recipe step into a shared notebook; apprentices replay those steps so service continues if the chef is absent. Finally, we preview trade-offs: physical replication gives an exact byte-for-byte copy, while logical replication lets you select which tables move between servers. By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe these options, state the WAL’s role, and decide when to prefer synchronous or asynchronous setups. Consider how your application would balance data loss risk and transaction latency.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Replication keeps copies of data to improve availability, scale reads, and support disaster recovery. The WAL is the mechanism that enables streaming replication.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives set clear outcomes for this chapter. First, you will explain why teams implement database replication in PostgreSQL: to enable high availability, to scale read workloads, and to provide disaster recovery. Understanding these motivations helps you choose the right replication architecture for your service-level goals. Second, you will differentiate physical and logical replication, including when an exact byte-for-byte copy is required and when selective table-level replication is better. Third, you will understand synchronous versus asynchronous replication: the guarantees each mode provides and the latency trade-offs involved. Finally, you will describe the role of the Write-Ahead Log and identify core streaming replication components. Each objective is practical: you will interpret configuration settings, reason about RPO and RTO, and inspect WAL-related parameters on a running PostgreSQL instance. This prepares you to plan a replication deployment, troubleshoot basic issues, and make informed trade-offs about data safety and performance.

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on demonstrable skills and the practical reasons they matter in production. You will be able to inspect WAL configuration with concrete commands and interpret results to decide whether streaming replication can be enabled. You will reason about max_wal_senders when adding multiple standbys, and you will understand how archive_mode and full_page_writes affect durability and backups. We will also practice framing choices by Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective so you can choose synchronous versus asynchronous modes intentionally. Inspect WAL settings
Use simple SQL to validate whether a server is ready for streaming replication.
psql -U postgres -d postgres
SHOW wal_level;
SHOW archive_mode;
SHOW max_wal_senders;
SHOW wal_log_hints;
SHOW full_page_writes;
Interpret: wal_level must be replica or logical; max_wal_senders must allow desired standbys.
Configuration implications
  • Change wal_level to enable streaming and restart the server.
  • Archive mode supports point-in-time recovery and complements replication.
  • full_page_writes protects against partial page writes during crashes.

screens.title: Why replicate? Availability, scaling, and recovery
screens.subtitle: The fundamental motivations for maintaining replicas of your database

narration.text: Replication begins with three practical problems that production systems face. First, high availability: if a primary server fails due to hardware or software faults, a standby can take over so applications continue serving requests. That reduces downtime and is essential for services with tight uptime targets. Second, read scaling: many applications read far more than they write. By routing read-only queries to standbys, you reduce contention on the primary and keep write latency low. Third, disaster recovery: a standby in a different geographic location acts as a recent copy you can promote if a disaster disables the primary site. To make these advantages concrete, think of a web application that serves product pages: if the primary handles both writes and all reads, peak traffic slows writes; adding standbys lets reads overflow to replicas and keeps purchases fast. Common misconceptions include assuming replication eliminates the need for backups—replicas can be corrupted or replicate accidental deletes—so archived WALs and backups remain necessary. Another misconception is that more replicas always improve safety; each replica adds operational complexity and potential lag. The key takeaway is to plan replication as part of a broader durability and availability strategy, matching replica count and placement to your RPO and RTO goals.

keyIdea.title: Motivation
keyIdea.text: Replication provides availability, read scaling, and disaster recovery but must be combined with backups and careful planning.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Why replicate?
Reasons to replicate
Availability, performance, and recovery are the core motivations for replication.
High availability
Standbys can be promoted to reduce downtime after failures.
Read scaling
Route read-only queries to standbys to preserve primary write performance.
Disaster recovery
Standbys provide geographically separate copies that can be promoted if needed.
Key Takeaway

Replication supports availability and scaling, but it does not replace backups or eliminate operational trade-offs.

Concrete example
An e-commerce catalog can serve product pages from standbys to handle read spikes while writes remain on the primary.
Common mistake
Assuming replicas remove the need for point-in-time backups. Replication duplicates mistakes and deletions unless WAL archives and backups are maintained.
Try this
List your application's RPO and RTO and map them to how many replicas and where they should be placed.

screens.title: Primary and Standby roles
screens.subtitle: Understanding roles, responsibilities, and read-only standbys

narration.text: PostgreSQL replication always involves role separation: a primary server and one or more standbys. The primary accepts all write activity and records every change in the Write-Ahead Log. Standbys receive those WAL records and replay them to maintain the same data state. Standbys are typically read-only when using physical streaming, which makes them excellent for read scaling and low-risk reporting queries. It’s important to grasp that a standby is not an independent writable copy in physical replication. A common misunderstanding is to treat a standby as a hot writable node; writing to a standby breaks the replication model and is not supported when the standby is a physical replica. Another detail is failover behavior: when a primary fails, a standby can be promoted to become the new primary. That promotion is the point where writes can resume there. Planning involves deciding which standbys are candidates for promotion, how to monitor WAL lag so you know how current a standby is, and whether to use synchronous standbys to reduce possible data loss. In short, roles are fixed by replication type: physical standbys are maintained by WAL replay and normally serve reads only; promotion converts a standby to primary in recovery scenarios.

keyIdea.title: Roles summary
keyIdea.text: Primary writes and streams WAL; standbys replay WAL and are usually read-only but can be promoted for failover.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Primary and Standby roles
Role hierarchy
Primary records WAL and serves writes; standbys replay WAL and serve reads.
Primary
Handles all writes and streams WAL to standbys. Single-write source in native streaming replication.
Standby
Replays WAL to remain synchronized and is typically used for read-only queries.
Promotion
When promoted, a standby becomes primary and can accept writes.
Concrete example
A reporting standby handles analytics queries while the primary continues to process transactional writes for orders.
Common misconception

A physical standby is not writable; attempting writes will lead to confusion and data divergence. For selective writable replicas, logical replication is used.

Key Takeaway

Identify promotion candidates and monitor WAL lag to ensure standbys are viable failover targets.

screens.title: Physical Replication (Streaming)
screens.subtitle: How WAL streaming creates an exact copy of the primary

narration.text: Physical replication, commonly called streaming replication in PostgreSQL, works by streaming Write-Ahead Log records from the primary to standbys. These WAL records contain every low-level change required to reconstruct the primary’s data files, so a standby maintained by replaying WAL will end up as a byte-for-byte copy of the primary. This approach is efficient and reliable for creating hot standbys suitable for promotion. A helpful way to picture physical replication is copying the entire recipe book page-for-page from a master chef to apprentices; apprentices cannot change recipes, they only replay what was recorded. Important limitations follow: physical standbys are read-only, you cannot replicate selective tables, and DDL or internal storage changes propagate as-is. Physical replication is ideal for disaster recovery and read scaling when you need an exact replica. Monitor WAL shipping and replay status to detect lag, which represents how far behind a standby is. A common operational pitfall is neglecting WAL archiving and max_wal_senders settings: if wal_level is minimal, streaming is impossible; max_wal_senders must accommodate the number of standbys and backup streams. Plan these parameters before creating base backups and starting streaming replication.

keyIdea.title: Physical replication essence
keyIdea.text: Streaming WAL creates an exact copy suitable for failover and read scaling but is read-only and not selective.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Physical Replication (Streaming)
Streaming via WAL
WAL records are streamed and replayed to produce a byte-for-byte copy.
Primary: write transaction → WAL
Stream WAL → standby receives WAL
Standby: replay WAL → data files updated
Promotion: standby becomes writable
Use base backups plus WAL streaming to create and maintain physical standbys.
Concrete example
A standby replays WAL continuously so that when a failover occurs it can be promoted and immediately accept writes with minimal data drift if synchronous is used.
Operational checklist
  • Ensure wal_level is replica or higher.
  • Set max_wal_senders high enough for your standbys.
  • Consider archive_mode for PITR in addition to streaming.
Key Takeaway

Physical streaming is efficient for exact copies and failover, but it is not flexible for selective replication.

screens.title: Logical Replication
screens.subtitle: Selective, row-level replication and its practical uses

narration.text: Logical replication operates at a higher level than physical replication. Instead of streaming raw WAL bytes, logical replication transmits the logical representation of changes — inserts, updates, and deletes — and applies those to subscribers. This gives you the flexibility to replicate individual tables, schemas, or even to replicate between different major PostgreSQL versions. Practical use cases include migrating data during an upgrade, selective replicas for analytics, and integrating PostgreSQL with heterogeneous systems. However, logical replication does not provide a byte-for-byte copy; it focuses on data changes and does not automatically propagate DDL in all cases. The trade-offs are clear: logical replication is more flexible but can be more resource-intensive and potentially slower for very high-volume write workloads because of the higher-level processing. A common misconception is that logical replication is always the best choice for multi-master setups; while logical replication can enable multi-master patterns, that architecture is complex and requires conflict resolution strategies not covered by native logical replication. When choosing logical replication, plan for schema compatibility, potential extra C P U for change decoding, and explicit handling of DDL changes.

keyIdea.title: Logical replication essence
keyIdea.text: Logical replication sends row-level changes, enabling selective replication and migrations, but it is less efficient for high-volume raw replication and requires care for DDL.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Logical Replication
Selective replication
Logical replication replicates data changes, enabling table-level or schema-level subscribers.
Use case: migrations
Stream changes to a new major version while both systems are writable in a controlled cutover.
Use case: analytics feeds
Subscribe to specific tables for downstream reporting systems without copying the entire database.
Concrete example
Replicate only customer and orders tables to an analytics cluster, leaving other tables out of the replication stream.
Common pitfall
Expecting DDL to replicate automatically. Logical replication focuses on row changes; schema changes may need manual coordination.
Key Takeaway

Choose logical replication when you need selective, cross-version, or multi-system replication and plan for schema handling and overhead.

screens.title: Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
screens.subtitle: Why WAL is fundamental for durability and replication

narration.text: The Write-Ahead Log is the central durability mechanism in PostgreSQL and the engine behind streaming replication. Every change — every insert, update, delete, and DDL operation — is recorded in the WAL before being applied to data files. This ordering guarantees that committed transactions can be recovered after a crash and that standbys can reconstruct the primary’s state by replaying WAL records. For replication, the primary streams WAL to standbys, and the standbys replay those same records so they remain synchronized. Understanding WAL also explains several configuration knobs: wal_level must be set to replica or logical to produce the necessary WAL records for streaming; max_wal_senders controls how many recipients the primary will stream to; archive_mode allows WAL files to be archived for point-in-time recovery. A misconception is thinking WAL is just a backup log — it is an operational stream used for both crash recovery and replication. In practice, monitoring WAL generation and shipping is crucial: excessive WAL can mean heavy write workloads, while lag in shipping indicates standbys falling behind. Knowing WAL's behavior lets you design replication with predictable recovery point objectives and backup strategies.

keyIdea.title: WAL summary
keyIdea.text: WAL records every change before it’s applied and is the substance that streaming replication ships and replays for durability and synchronization.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
WAL: the replication fuel
Every change is recorded in WAL before being written to data files; standbys replay WAL to stay synchronized.
WAL sequence: transaction produces WAL → WAL is written and flushed → primary may stream WAL to standby → standby replays WAL to update files.
Configuration knobs
  • wal_level: must be replica or logical for replication.
  • max_wal_senders: number of concurrent WAL streams allowed.
  • archive_mode: if on, WAL files are archived for PITR.
Concrete example
If wal_level is minimal, streaming replication cannot operate; changing it to replica and restarting enables streaming generation of WAL data for standbys.
Key Takeaway

WAL is central: configure wal_level, max_wal_senders, and archive_mode appropriately to support streaming replication and backups.

screens.title: Streaming Replication Architecture
screens.subtitle: Core components and how they interact in native streaming replication

narration.text: Native streaming replication in PostgreSQL is composed of a small set of cooperating components. The primary writes WAL records and maintains a WAL sender process for each connected standby or backup stream. Each standby runs a WAL receiver process to accept streamed WAL and a replay mechanism to apply those WAL records to its local data files. A base backup or pg_basebackup is typically used to create an initial copy of the primary's data directory before starting continuous streaming. The important architectural pieces are WAL senders on the primary, WAL receivers on standbys, base backups for initial sync, and optionally archive storage for WAL segments to support point-in-time recovery. Monitoring metrics to watch include WAL send/receive status and replay progress to measure lag. Architecturally, consider network paths and disk throughput because streaming and replay both consume input and output and bandwidth. If you plan to have multiple standbys, ensure max_wal_senders is set accordingly. This architecture produces a robust pipeline: changes written once at the primary are replayed by many standbys to provide availability and read scaling. Always document promotion procedures and ensure your monitoring covers replay lag and WAL archive health.

keyIdea.title: Architecture snapshot
keyIdea.text: Primary WAL senders, standby WAL receivers and replay, plus base backups and optional WAL archives form the streaming replication pipeline.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Streaming Replication Architecture
Components
Primary: WAL senders
Sends WAL to standby receivers and handles writes.
Standby: WAL receiver & replay
Receives WAL and applies changes to match primary.
Base backup
Initial copy used to bootstrap standbys before continuous streaming.
WAL archive
Optional storage of WAL files for PITR and recovery beyond live stream.
Concrete scenario
Set max_wal_senders to 3 if you plan three concurrent standbys; use pg_basebackup to create the initial data copy before connecting WAL streams.
Monitoring focus
  • WAL send/receive status.
  • Replay lag on standbys.
  • WAL archive success if enabled.
Key Takeaway

Design the pipeline from base backup to continuous WAL streaming and monitor send/receive/replay to ensure replicas are viable.

screens.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication
screens.subtitle: Choosing between zero-data-loss and minimal latency

narration.text: Synchronous and asynchronous replication differ in when a primary considers a transaction committed. In asynchronous replication the primary commits and continues without waiting for confirmation that standbys have received or flushed the WAL. This gives the primary lower latency and high throughput, but it opens a small window where committed transactions on the primary might not exist on standbys if the primary crashes before shipping or flushing WAL. Many systems accept this trade-off for performance. Synchronous replication requires at least one standby to confirm receipt and flush of WAL before the primary marks the transaction committed, guaranteeing zero data loss for that synchronous standby. The cost is increased transaction latency equal to the network round-trip and flush time to the standby. Choosing between modes depends on Recovery Point Objective: if zero data loss is essential, use synchronous replication and accept higher latencies; if low write latency is critical and small data loss is tolerable, choose asynchronous replication. A common misconception is thinking synchronous removes all risk — misconfigured synchronous settings or network partitions can block commits, so plan for quorum rules and monitor for blocked transactions.

keyIdea.title: Sync mode trade-off
keyIdea.text: Synchronous ensures zero data loss at the cost of latency; asynchronous favors performance with small potential data loss.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Synchronous vs Asynchronous
Asynchronous
Primary does not wait for standby confirmation; best for performance where small data loss is acceptable.
Pros: low primary latency, high throughput. Cons: possible small data loss if primary fails.
Synchronous
Primary waits for at least one standby to confirm WAL receipt and flush before commit; best for zero data loss guarantees.
Pros: zero data loss w.r.t configured standbys. Cons: added latency, risk of blocking under network issues.
Concrete scenario
If RPO is zero, configure synchronous replication and accept higher commit latency. If RPO is minutes, asynchronous may be acceptable.
Key Takeaway

Align sync mode with recovery objectives; monitor for blocked commits and plan network redundancy if using synchronous replication.

screens.title: Choosing a Replication Strategy
screens.subtitle: A simple decision process using RPO and workload characteristics

narration.text: Choosing a replication approach requires balancing data safety, performance, and operational complexity. Start by stating your Recovery Point Objective: how much data loss, measured in time, can you tolerate? If your RPO is zero, synchronous replication is the only way to guarantee no data loss for committed transactions. Next, examine your workload: if writes are heavy and latency-sensitive, asynchronous physical replication usually preserves primary performance while offering read scaling. If you need selective replication — for example, replicating only certain tables to a reporting cluster or migrating between major versions — logical replication is the right tool even though it may use more C P U and be slower at high write volumes. Consider operational needs: do you require fast promotion and identical replicas, or flexible topology across versions? Finally, plan infrastructure: set wal_level accordingly, provision max_wal_senders for expected standbys, and decide on archive_mode for PITR. A recommended process is: define RPO/RTO → choose physical vs logical → choose sync mode → set WAL and sender parameters → prepare base backups and monitoring. This process connects requirements to configuration choices and helps prevent surprises during failover or upgrades.

keyIdea.title: Decision flow
keyIdea.text: Map RPO and workload to a replication type and sync mode, then configure WAL and senders, bootstrap with a base backup, and monitor.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Choosing a Replication Strategy
Step-by-step
1. Define RPO/RTO
Decide acceptable data loss and recovery time.
2. Choose replication type
Physical for exact copies; logical for selective replication or cross-version migration.
3. Select sync mode
Synchronous for zero data loss; asynchronous for better primary performance.
4. Configure WAL and senders
Set wal_level, max_wal_senders, and archive_mode as needed.
Concrete example
If RPO = 0 and write latency tolerance exists, pick synchronous physical replication and ensure network latency is minimized between primary and standby.
Key Takeaway

Follow a requirements-first flow: requirements → replication type → sync mode → configuration → monitoring.

screens.title: Inspecting WAL Configuration
screens.subtitle: Run basic checks that determine readiness for streaming replication

narration.text: This activity shows how to inspect WAL-related settings that determine whether a PostgreSQL server is ready for streaming replication. Connect to your PostgreSQL 12 primary using psql and run a few SHOW commands to review wal_level, archive_mode, max_wal_senders, wal_log_hints, and full_page_writes. These values tell you whether the server is producing the WAL records required for streaming, whether WAL is being archived for PITR, and whether enough WAL sender slots are allocated for standbys. If wal_level is minimal, streaming will fail; change it to replica or logical as needed and restart PostgreSQL. If you plan three standbys, increase max_wal_senders accordingly so the primary can maintain three concurrent WAL sender processes. Also check full_page_writes and wal_log_hints because they affect base backup and crash-safety behavior. This exercise does not change configuration, but it trains you to interpret the output and make a configuration plan. After checking, reflect on what values you would change and why, and which standbys you would designate as synchronous candidates. This understanding bridges conceptual replication choices with concrete server settings. Inspecting WAL Configuration means use psql show commands to inspect wal readiness: wal_level, archive_mode, max_wal_senders, wal_log_hints, and full_page_writes.. In practical terms, run basic checks that determine readiness for streaming replication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity summary
keyIdea.text: Use psql SHOW commands to inspect WAL readiness: wal_level, archive_mode, max_wal_senders, wal_log_hints, and full_page_writes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Inspecting WAL Configuration
Starter commands
Open psql as postgres and run these checks to understand WAL state.
psql -U postgres -d postgres
SHOW wal_level;
SHOW archive_mode;
SHOW max_wal_senders;
SHOW wal_log_hints;
SHOW full_page_writes;
If wal_level returns 'replica', streaming is supported. If it returns 'minimal', you cannot stream WAL.
Interpreting results
  • archive_mode = on → WAL segments are archived for PITR.
  • max_wal_senders numeric → number of concurrent standby connections allowed.
  • full_page_writes = on → safer base backups and crash recovery behavior.
Concrete reflection
If you plan three standbys, consider setting max_wal_senders to 5 to leave room for backup processes. If wal_level is minimal, prepare to change it to replica and restart the server.
Key Takeaway

Knowing these settings bridges replication strategy and actual server readiness; inspect before you attempt to create standbys.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pro Tips
screens.subtitle: Operational traps to avoid and tips to keep replication healthy

narration.text: When operating replication, a few recurring mistakes surface across teams. First, failing to set wal_level appropriately before attempting streaming. If wal_level is minimal you will not generate the WAL necessary for replicas to catch up. Second, under-provisioning max_wal_senders so that new standbys or backup streams cannot connect. Third, treating replicas as substitutes for backups: replication mirrors mistakes and deletions, so maintain WAL archives and regular backups for point-in-time recovery. Fourth, assuming synchronous replication is a panacea; it guarantees no data loss for waiting standbys but can lead to blocked commits if network or standby input and output is slow. Pro tips: use a monitoring solution that reports WAL send/receive status and replay lag, designate at least one standby as a promotion candidate and test promotion procedures regularly, and enable archive_mode if you need PITR. Also, when planning multiple standbys, consider placement to reduce network latency for synchronous standbys. Finally, document your configuration changes and test failover paths in a staging environment before relying on them in production. These operational practices dramatically reduce friction when troubles occur. Common Mistakes and Pro Tips means avoid configuration oversights and test failover paths; maintain archives and backups because replication does not replace them.. In practical terms, operational traps to avoid and tips to keep replication healthy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.title: Operations insight
keyIdea.text: Avoid configuration oversights and test failover paths; maintain archives and backups because replication does not replace them.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Common Mistakes and Pro Tips
Common mistakes
  • Not setting wal_level to replica or logical before streaming.
  • Insufficient max_wal_senders for planned standbys.
  • Relying on replicas instead of maintaining archives and backups.
  • Assuming synchronous replication eliminates operational risk.
Pro tips
  • Monitor WAL send/receive and replay lag continuously.
  • Test promotion and failover in a staging environment.
  • Reserve enough max_wal_senders for growth and backup processes.
  • Place synchronous standbys with low network latency to reduce commit delay.
Pitfall to avoid
Configuring synchronous replication without redundancy can cause service stalls during network partitions; plan quorum and failover behavior carefully.
Key Takeaway

Operational discipline—correct WAL settings, monitoring, backups, and tested promotion—keeps replication reliable.

narration.text: These concise concept cards restate the most important ideas to carry forward. Replication is the process of maintaining multiple copies of a database so that changes on a primary propagate to standbys for availability, read scaling, and disaster recovery. The primary server is the single write source in native streaming replication; standbys replay WAL records to remain synchronized and are typically read-only until promotion. Physical replication streams WAL at a low level to give an exact copy while logical replication sends row-level changes for selective replication and migrations. Keep these simple definitions in mind as mental anchors when designing replication topologies and diagnosing issues. narration.text: This concluding set of concept cards captures the technical terms you will see in configuration and troubleshooting. Physical replication streams WAL records to create a byte-for-byte standby. Logical replication transmits row-level changes for selective replication and migration scenarios. The Write-Ahead Log is the record every change writes first, and WAL-related parameters like wal_level, max_wal_senders, and archive_mode determine your ability to stream WAL and support point-in-time recovery. Finally, remember the distinction between synchronous and asynchronous modes: synchronous waits for standby confirmation to prevent data loss while asynchronous favors primary performance.
